content.title: Team USA’s Mark DeRosa on tough calls, managing for the first time in WBC
content.text: AL East Blue Jays Orioles Rays Red Sox Yankees AL Central Guardians Royals Tigers Twins White Sox AL West Angels Astros Athletics Mariners Rangers NL East Braves Marlins Mets Nationals Phillies NL Central Brewers Cardinals Cubs Pirates Reds NL West Diamondbacks Dodgers Giants Padres Rockies Scores & Schedule Standings Podcasts The Windup Newsletter Fantasy MLB Prospects MLB Odds MLB Picks Power Rankings Fans Speak Up Top Prospects Q&A Team USA’s Mark DeRosa on tough calls, managing for the first time in WBC Share full article 14 Mark DeRosa has never managed a baseball game. Over the course of a long season, with time to learn and the value of any individual game relatively minor, that might not be such a hindrance. But with no such room for error, the former major-leaguer will man the top step of the dugout for the first time in the World Baseball Classic , and every move he makes leading Team USA will have an outsized impact on the team’s ability to defend its WBC title. When should he pull a starter, and when he does, to which reliever should he turn? When should he shift, when should he call for a steal and when, even with his lineup of All-Stars, should he pinch-hit? The game tends to speed up when those decisions are yours to make, but DeRosa slowed down before Team USA’s first exhibition Wednesday to talk to The Athletic about his managerial philosophy. In this tournament, the decisions you make in a game have extra importance. You have a lot of playing experience but not much calling the shots, so how do you prepare for that? When I got named the manager of this team, it was late August. I managed probably 60 games in my apartment throughout the course of following the end of the season and the postseason. I put a piece of paper in front of me with the Phillies and the Astros lineups and I tried to think along with (Houston manager) Dusty Baker and (Phillies manager) Rob Thomson. I think the game is won and lost on the mound; I always have. There’s just too many monsters on this team to not want to go to somebody in the bullpen. That’s the biggest thing. That was one of my messages to them. Nobody has to give in. There can’t be any give-in with this pitching staff. There’s no reason to. You have some coaches on your staff with a lot of experience — Dino Ebel, Dave Righetti, Jerry Manuel. How much do you lean on them? I’m going to lean on them huge. Playing against Aaron Boone and the A.J. Hinches and the Alex Coras and the Dave Robertses … Phil Nevin was a teammate of mine. I’ve called a ton and they’ve said, “Listen, regardless of whether you’ve done it before or not done it before, the biggest thing is the game is going to get fast on you. Lean on the guys next to you.” Jerry Manuel’s won more than 700 games. Andy Pettitte’s got 19 postseason wins. Dave Righetti’s got three World Series out there. I am not one who doesn’t want to pick the brains of the guys around me to make these decisions. You have certain restrictions in this tournament in terms of how long starters can go each round and how often relievers can pitch. Does that make it harder to make decisions throughout a game, or is it almost easier because some options will simply be removed from the board? It’s both. I talked to all the pitching coaches who had these guys — what makes them tick, how to get the best out of them. Who can come in with a dirty inning and who needs a clean inning, and who can go back-to-back. Probably no one’s going to go back-to-back days in pool play. There’s just no reason to, and the way the schedule lines up, the only way someone potentially would is in the semifinals and the finals. Let’s hope we get there. In talking to Jim Leyland about this, because he managed it in ’17, he said, “Do not script it. Plan it.” Your script could blow up in your face super quick. You want to be ready to make the right move. That being said, there’s pitch limits and pitch counts and all that stuff. I would think it would make it a little bit easier. You have some very veteran pitchers on your roster who have accomplished a lot in this game. But your bullpen is also loaded. How will you weigh going to the bullpen early versus giving some of these starters the rope they’ve earned over their careers? In order to get through this, these guys are going to have to get their pitches in. There’s no question about that. You can’t cover all the innings if our starters don’t give us a little bit of length. As you were managing those games along with Dusty and Rob Thomson in your living room during the World Series, how did you do? How often were you thinking along the same track as they were? I was kind of in-between both of them. Dusty’s a guy who has a lot of trust. I might have done things a little quicker than him. Rob Thomson let you know their philosophy in Games 1 and 2, that he was going to be quick to the ’pen. Yordan Alvarez was never going to not see José Alvarado. But the player in me says if you show me those bullpen guys enough in a series, eventually toward the end, somebody’s going to clip them. Unfortunately for the Phillies, that’s what happened. They’re both phenomenal managers. I was just trying to think along with them. At the end of that experience, did you realize things about your own managerial philosophy? You’ve got to trust yourself. I played 13 and a half years in the big leagues. I’ve been in every situation this game has to offer. I also understand that I’ve never been in this position before. I’m humbled and honored by it, but I plan on sticking my nose in and getting after it.
